scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

message.reasoning:
The scenario describes a man who did not have an emotional reaction (specifically, did not cry) upon seeing his bride on their wedding day, despite her expectations based on social media posts. He focused on her and smiled, but did not break down in tears. The bride expressed disappointment, and the man defended his reaction, questioning the emphasis on performance. The question is whether his action (not being emotional) is morally acceptable.

Moral acceptability here hinges on whether there is a moral obligation to display certain emotions on one's wedding day, particularly to meet a partner's expectations. The man did not act disrespectfully; he smiled and was clearly happy to marry her. His reaction was genuine, even if not as dramatic as some social media portrayals. The bride's disappointment stems from unmet expectations, but that does not necessarily make his lack of tears morally wrong. He did not intend to hurt her; he simply did not have that specific emotional response. Moreover, the maid of honor's nudging added pressure, which he rightly objected to.

The core issue is whether one is morally obligated to perform emotions for the sake of a partner's fantasy. Authenticity in emotional expression is generally valued, and forcing emotions can be seen as inauthentic or even manipulative. The man's response was honest, and he communicated his feelings after the fact. While empathy for his wife's feelings is important, his action itself—being less emotional—does not rise to the level of moral wrongdoing. It might be a relational misstep or a cause for communication, but not morally unacceptable.

Therefore, the action is morally acceptable. Answer: 1
